2016 Election Results: County-level Study and Analysis¶

Stat 4770 Final Project¶

  • Bharat Elango

Introduction¶

In this project, we will be looking at the 2016 Election results by each county and who they voted for: the Democratic or Republican party.¶

Our dataset provides us with a myriad of variables collected for each county, alongside which party that county voted for in 2016.¶

For this project, we will be:¶

  • Analyzing these results to see the difference in living qualities between counties that voted for different parties.
  • Understanding the relationship between the various environmental social determinants collected in each county.
  • Finally, we will answer our question of whether economic hardship can predict whether a county will vote Republican or Democratic with a Decision Tree.

First, let us get a refresher on what happened in the 2016 elections, and understand our data with some Exploratory Data Analysis!¶

Background¶

As a background, the 2016 election was won by Donald Trump over Hillary Clinton, and as seen in these figures, it seemed to be by a huge landslide, or was it?¶

It is important to remember that, counties are not the same as people. While more counties voted Republican, more people live in Democratic-won counties (about 55%), consistent with Clinton winning the popular vote.¶

Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)¶

The county-level data we have gives many possible variables to use:¶

Uninsured, Primary.Care.Physicians.Per.1000, Mental.health.providers.Per.1000
Adult.Obesity, Proportion.of.Smokers, High.School.Graduation
Insufficient.Sleep, Physical.Inactivity, Excessive.Drinking
Median.Household.Income, Severe.Housing.Problems, Unemployment
Food.Insecurity.Quintile, Income.Inequality.Quartile, Percent.Rural
Over.65, Percent.Females, Life.Expectancy
Population
  • For this project, we will be primarily focusing on the variables describing the environmental determinants of health/economic hardships, but also look at demographic characteristics for some of our questions.

Let's do some EDA on the relationship between the variables we are focused on against each other and against the Election Results!¶

  • Severe housing problems: This variable separates the parties best; blue and red are much more separable along it than along any other variable.
  • Income: Blue (Democrat) counties are more spread out, including both poor and rich counties.
  • Unemployment and uninsured rate: Barely separate the parties; blue and red overlap almost completely.
  • Between variables: Income falls as unemployment and uninsured rate rise, while housing problems is mostly unrelated to income.
  • Overall: No single variable separates the parties on its own, which is why we will turn to a tree.

Research Topic and Question¶

Now that we got a good background, let's go into our actual questions:¶

  1. Which party is more desirable for a wealthier county?
  2. Does a state's proportion of women relate to its proportion of Democratic counties?
  3. Does the 2016 Election data follow the Urban-Rural political divide phenomenon?
  4. Can economic hardship variables predict a county's party? (We will answer this with a Decision Tree!)

Question 1 Hypothesis:¶

Hypothesis: Wealthier counties, wanting to keep their money, will vote for less extreme taxation, siding with the Republican party, and, in turn, less wealthy counties will want to decrease the income inequality, therefore voting for the Democratic party.¶

Let us look at the median household income in each county split by their winning party.¶

What we see is that the Democratic voting counties have a slightly higher median houshold income. Can we, therefore, reject the hypothesis and say that wealthier counties will vote Democratic?¶
NO¶
This is too far of a reach from our current plot, as the median of the Democratic voting counties is only modestly higher, and we can already see an issue with the Democratic voting county's plot having a much higher variance, so let us look a bit deeper.¶

Here, we see that the Democratic voting counties are not wealthier overall, but include the poorest and richest counties.¶

  • The middle income decile of these Democratic voting counties is much less prevalent than either extremes of rich and poor counties
  • So rejecting the hypothesis is inconclusive, since a higher wealth of a county does not directly relate to voting for the Democratic party as a large amount of poorer counties also voted Democratic.

Question 2 Hypothesis:¶

It has been known that, since the 1980s, politics has become more polarized based on sex. Men have been seen to lean more Republican and women lean more Democratic. We want to test this.¶

HUGE ASSUMPTION: Since we do not have data of what proportion of women voted, just the proportion of women living in the county, we are assuming the proportion of women living in the county is correlated with the proportion of women who voted in the county, which will allow us to test this question, but is a large assumption to make.¶

Hypothesis: States more comprised of women will have more counties voting Democratic, while states less comprised of women will have more counties voting Republican.¶

  • We see that there is a direct correlation between the percent of women in a state to percent of counties that voted Democrat in the state, albeit not a significant one, as seen by the p-value of 0.1503.

  • This hypothesis seems to be grounded in some truth despite not being significant as we do see our regression line trending upwards, with a slope of 7.82.

Question 3 Hypothesis:¶

Our next question tests a well-known phenomenon called the Urban-Rural Political Divide phenomenon, in that urban regions typically lean liberally/democratic, as a result of increased diversity, while rural regions lean republican.¶

Hypothesis: More urban counties will vote Democratic while more rural counties will vote Republican.¶

P-value: 1.6286229520438952e-64

  • This is a very large difference; the median Republican county is about 59% rural, while the median Democrat county is only about 17% rural.

  • We can confidently reject the null hypothesis of there being no difference in the percentage of rural population between Republican and Democratic counties, as seen by the P-value of 1.629e-64.

Question 4: Decision Tree¶

We will now utilize a Decision Tree to attempt prediction of which party a county voted for based on their economic hardship and the variables that coincide with this.¶

The continuous variables we will be using are:¶

  • Median Household Income
  • Severe Housing Problems (Higher means worse)
  • Unemployment
  • Uninsured

The categorical variables we will be using are:¶

  • Food Insecurity Quintile
  • Income Inequality Quartile

This is our Decision Tree¶

But what does it mean?¶

Some important parts to understand is:¶

  • A blue node means the predictor expects the county that falls in that node to be more Democratic, and red is Republican.
  • The value in each box is the share of counties in it that are Democrat and Republican, in that order, so the far left box showing [0.036, 0.964] means that 96.4% of the counties in it voted Republican.
  • Counties with severe housing problems below about 15% make up 60% of all counties and are 96% Republican, so this one rule sorts most of the counties.
  • Among counties with high housing problems (above 17.5%), the higher-income ones (above about $56,500) are 77% Democrat.
  • Lower-income counties with high housing problems that are in the most unequal quartile and have an uninsured rate below about 14% are about 69% Democrat, which fits our earlier finding that the poorest counties also lean Democrat.
  • Unemployment and food insecurity only appear deep in the tree, in small groups of counties, so they add little to the predictions.

Here we have our variables ranked by importance for prediction of whether the county will vote of obtained from our tree.¶

As we saw before in our pairplot, our Severe.Housing.Problems ended up being the best predictor for which party a county will vote for, with Median.Household.Income in 2nd, and the rest being much weaker predictors.¶

Now, let's try using some data the tree has not seen yet and see whether the tree accurately guesses what party the counties voted for.¶

  • The tree is right for about 87.8% of counties it has never seen, compared with 84.3% for always guessing Republican.
  • It is very good at spotting Republican counties (432 of 458 correct), but it only finds about half of the Democrat counties (45 of 85).

Conclusions¶

  • For Question 1, it is not a simple case of wealthy counties voting Republican, since the share of Democrat counties is highest at both the poorest and richest ends of the income scale and lowest in the middle.
  • For Question 2, there is a weak upward trend between the percent of women in a state and its share of Democrat counties, but it is not statistically significant (p-value = 0.1503), and this data cannot tell us how women actually voted.
  • For Question 3, the urban-rural divide is supported by the findings, as Democrat counties are far less rural than Republican counties (a median of about 17% compared with about 59%), which is very unlikely to be due to chance.
  • For Question 4, the decision tree found severe housing problems and median income to be the most important variables, and it correctly predicted about 87.8% of unseen counties compared with 84.3% from always guessing Republican, but it only found about half of the Democrat counties.
  • It is important to note that these results are county-level associations from a single election, so they do not show causation.
